---
title: "Precision–recall curves"
description: "Evaluating the flagged cases when positives are rare: PR curves, average precision, precision and lift in the top k%, and the role of the base rate."
---

```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from modelperf.metrics import (
    auc_rank,
    average_precision,
    pr_points,
    roc_points,
    threshold_metrics,
    top_share_metrics,
)
from modelperf.models import binary_predictions
from modelperf.plots import INK_SECONDARY, MODEL_COLORS, MUTED, SURFACE, plot_pr, use_style

use_style()
b = binary_predictions()
y = b["y"]
rate = y.mean()
models = ("GLM", "GBM")
auc = {m: auc_rank(y, b[m]) for m in models}
ap = {m: average_precision(y, b[m]) for m in models}
```

**Question answered:** of the cases the model flags, how many are real
positives, and how many of the real positives does it find?

## Why look beyond ROC

The [ROC curve](roc-auc.qmd) measures false alarms *relative to all
negatives*: the false positive rate is FP / (FP + TN). With
`{python} f"{1 - rate:.1%}"` of policies without a claim, that denominator is
huge, and a small false positive rate can hide a large number of false alarms:

```{python}
#| include: false
m10 = threshold_metrics(y, b["GBM"], 0.1)
c10 = (m10["false positive rate"] * (y == 0).sum(), m10["recall (TPR)"] * (y == 1).sum())
```

At a threshold of 0.1, the GBM has a false positive rate of only
`{python} f"{m10['false positive rate']:.1%}"`: a point far to the left on the
ROC curve. But that is `{python} f"{c10[0]:,.0f}"` false alarms against
`{python} f"{c10[1]:,.0f}"` correctly flagged claims, so only
`{python} f"{m10['precision']:.0%}"` of the flagged policies actually have a
claim.

**Precision** relates false alarms to true hits instead of to all negatives,
so it shows directly what happens among the flagged cases. That makes it the
natural metric when positives are rare and attention goes to the cases the
model flags: fraud checks, claim reviews, medical screening, marketing
campaigns.

## The precision–recall curve

The PR curve uses the same threshold sweep as the ROC curve, but plots

- **recall** (true positive rate: the share of all claims we flag) on the
  x-axis, against
- **precision** (the share of flagged policies with a claim) on the y-axis.

Starting from a very high threshold, only the highest-risk policies are
flagged: recall is small and, for a good model, precision is high. Lowering the
threshold raises recall and, usually, lowers precision, until everything is
flagged: recall 1 and precision equal to the overall claim rate.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pr
#| fig-cap: "Precision–recall curves on the test set. Thin gray curves connect points with the same F1 score."
ax = plot_pr(y, {m: b[m] for m in models}, ylim=0.5)
```

Three things differ from a ROC plot:

- **The baseline is the claim rate, not a diagonal.** Flagging at random gives
  a precision equal to the claim rate (`{python} f"{rate:.1%}"`) at every recall.
- **The curve isn't monotone.** Precision can go up *or* down when the
  threshold drops, so the curve is jagged, especially on the left where few
  policies are flagged and each one changes precision noticeably.
- **The left part matters most.** It shows the highest-risk policies, which is
  where a review or intervention would start. Here the GBM clearly beats the
  GLM, even though their ROC curves were close.

```{python}
#| include: false
def best_f1(m):
    """Highest F1 over all thresholds, and the threshold where it is reached."""
    pr = pr_points(y, b[m])
    f1 = 2 * pr["precision"] * pr["recall"] / (pr["precision"] + pr["recall"])
    return f1.max(), pr.loc[f1.idxmax(), "threshold"]
f1 = {m: best_f1(m) for m in models}
```

The gray curves connect points of equal **F1 score**, the harmonic mean of
precision and recall. The best F1 the GBM reaches is
`{python} f"{f1['GBM'][0]:.3f}"` (at threshold `{python} f"{f1['GBM'][1]:.2f}"`),
against `{python} f"{f1['GLM'][0]:.3f}"` for the GLM. Low values like these are
typical for rare events. F1 is only a convenient summary: it weights precision
and recall equally, which rarely matches the actual costs of misses and false
alarms.

## Average precision

**Average precision** (AP) condenses the PR curve into one number: the
precision at each threshold, weighted by how much recall that threshold adds,

$$
\text{AP} = \sum_k (R_k - R_{k-1})\, P_k,
$$

where $R_k$ and $P_k$ are recall and precision after lowering the threshold
past the $k$-th distinct score. The Null model's AP equals the claim rate.

Using the same ten toy policies as on the ROC page:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-toy-pr
#| tbl-cap: "Precision and recall of the ten toy policies, and each threshold's contribution to AP."
#| code-fold: false
toy_y = np.array([1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0])
toy_p = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.55, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1])
toy = pr_points(toy_y, toy_p)
toy["AP contribution"] = np.diff(np.r_[0, toy["recall"]]) * toy["precision"]
toy.round(3)
```

```{python}
#| include: false
toy_ap = toy["AP contribution"].sum()
toy_trap = np.trapezoid(np.r_[1.0, toy["precision"]], np.r_[0.0, toy["recall"]])
```

Only the thresholds that add a claim contribute, each with weight 1/4. The AP is
`{python} f"{toy_ap:.3f}"`: on average, when the threshold passes a policy with a
claim, `{python} f"{toy_ap:.0%}"` of the flagged policies have a claim.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Don't use the trapezoidal area
Computing the area under the PR curve with the trapezoidal rule (as for ROC)
connects the points with straight lines. Between two PR points, precision does
not change linearly, so the result is off, in either direction, and it also
depends on which starting point is assumed at recall 0. On the toy example it
gives `{python} f"{toy_trap:.3f}"` instead of `{python} f"{toy_ap:.3f}"`. With
many distinct scores the gap shrinks, but AP is the well-defined summary:
`average_precision_score` in scikit-learn, whereas `sklearn.metrics.auc` on a
PR curve is the trapezoidal version.
:::

## ROC and PR tell different stories

```{python}
#| label: tbl-auc-ap
#| tbl-cap: "Ranking metrics of both models. 'AP / claim rate' shows how many times better than random the average precision is."
pd.DataFrame({
    "AUC": auc,
    "Average precision": ap,
    "AP / claim rate": {m: ap[m] / rate for m in models},
}).round(3)
```

The GBM's AUC is `{python} f"{auc['GBM'] - auc['GLM']:.3f}"` higher than the
GLM's, a modest `{python} f"{auc['GBM'] / auc['GLM'] - 1:.0%}"`. Its average
precision is `{python} f"{ap['GBM'] / ap['GLM'] - 1:.0%}"` higher. Both metrics
summarize the same ranking, but they weight it differently:

- **AUC** weighs all pairs of a claim and a non-claim equally, wherever they
  are in the ranking.
- **AP** weighs the top of the ranking most: a claim ranked first raises
  precision at every later threshold.

The GBM's advantage is concentrated in its highest-risk predictions, so AP
shows it more clearly.

## Precision and lift in the top k%

In practice, capacity is often fixed: 'we can review 5% of policies'. Then
the relevant question is how good the top 5% of the ranking is. Two measures
answer it:

- **precision at k%**: the share of flagged policies with a claim, and
- **lift at k%**: precision divided by the overall claim rate, i.e. how many
  times more claims the flagged group contains than a random group of the same
  size.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-top-k
#| tbl-cap: "Flagging the k% of policies with the highest predicted probability."
shares = [0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20]
top = pd.concat(
    {m: pd.DataFrame({f"top {s:.0%}": top_share_metrics(y, b[m], s) for s in shares}).T for m in models},
    axis=1,
)
top.round(3)
```

```{python}
#| include: false
t1 = {m: top_share_metrics(y, b[m], 0.01) for m in models}
```

Flagging the top 1%, the GBM finds `{python} f"{t1['GBM']['lift']:.1f}"` times
more claims than random selection would, the GLM
`{python} f"{t1['GLM']['lift']:.1f}"` times. As the flagged share grows,
precision falls towards the claim rate and lift towards 1. Showing lift for
every decile of the ranking gives a **lift chart**, the subject of a later
page.

## Precision depends on the claim rate

Precision has a property that matters a lot in practice: unlike the ROC curve,
it **depends on the base rate**. At any threshold,

$$
\text{precision} = \frac{\pi \cdot \text{TPR}}{\pi \cdot \text{TPR} + (1 - \pi) \cdot \text{FPR}},
$$

where $\pi$ is the share of positives. TPR and FPR are properties of the model
alone. Precision mixes them with $\pi$. To see the effect, we keep all policies
with a claim and randomly drop policies without a claim until the claim rate
reaches 10%, 20% and 50%. The model and its ranking don't change.

```{python}
#| code-fold: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
pos, neg = np.flatnonzero(y == 1), np.flatnonzero(y == 0)
samples = {}
for target in (rate, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50):
    n_neg = min(len(neg), int(len(pos) * (1 - target) / target))
    idx = np.r_[pos, rng.choice(neg, n_neg, replace=False)]
    samples[f"{target:.1%}"] = (y.to_numpy()[idx], b["GBM"].to_numpy()[idx])
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-prevalence
#| fig-cap: "The same GBM evaluated at different claim rates (by subsampling policies without a claim). Left: ROC curves. Right: precision–recall curves."
ramp = ["#86b6ef", "#3987e5", "#1c5cab", "#0d366b"]  # light to dark: rising claim rate
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.6))
axes[0].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], color=MUTED, linewidth=1)
for (label, (ys, ps)), color in zip(samples.items(), ramp):
    roc, pr = roc_points(ys, ps), pr_points(ys, ps)
    axes[0].plot(roc["fpr"], roc["tpr"], color=color, label=f"claim rate {label} (AUC {auc_rank(ys, ps):.3f})")
    axes[1].plot(np.r_[0, pr["recall"]], np.r_[pr["precision"].iloc[0], pr["precision"]],
                 drawstyle="steps-pre", color=color, label=f"claim rate {label} (AP {average_precision(ys, ps):.3f})")
axes[0].set(xlabel="False positive rate", ylabel="True positive rate", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1.01), aspect="equal")
axes[1].set(xlabel="Recall", ylabel="Precision", xlim=(0, 1), ylim=(0, 1.01))
axes[0].legend(loc="lower right")
axes[1].legend(loc="upper right")
fig.tight_layout()
```

```{python}
#| include: false
ap_by_rate = {k: average_precision(*v) for k, v in samples.items()}
```

The ROC curves lie on top of each other: AUC doesn't change. The PR curves rise
with the claim rate, and AP climbs from `{python} f"{ap_by_rate[f'{rate:.1%}']:.2f}"`
to `{python} f"{ap_by_rate['50.0%']:.2f}"`. **Same model, same ranking,
different AP.** This has practical consequences:

- **Don't compare AP across datasets, segments or time periods with different
  base rates.** A higher AP may only mean more positives. Report the base rate
  next to every AP, or report AP / base rate.
- **Balanced test sets inflate precision.** Undersampling negatives, common in
  fraud and medical studies, makes precision look far better than it will be in
  production.
- **Precision drifts when the base rate drifts.** If the claim rate drops next
  year, the precision of the same model at the same threshold drops too, even
  though nothing about the model has changed. This is one reason to monitor the
  base rate along with model metrics.

## ROC or PR?

The two curves contain the same information (given the base rate, every ROC
point maps to exactly one PR point), but they emphasize different things:

| | ROC / AUC | PR / AP |
|---|---|---|
| Focus | the whole ranking, both classes | the top of the ranking, positive class |
| False alarms measured relative to | all negatives | true hits |
| Depends on base rate | no | yes |
| Random baseline | 0.5 | base rate |
| Good for | comparing rankings across populations; when both error types matter | rare positives where only the flagged cases are acted on |

It's often claimed that AP is 'the right metric for imbalanced data'. That's
too simple. Imbalance alone doesn't make AUC wrong. Recent work (McDermott et
al., 2024) shows that AP favors improvements at the top of the ranking and can
favor models that work best for the subgroups with the highest base rates.
**Choose by the question**: use AUC when the whole ranking matters, AP or
precision at k% when only the top of the ranking is acted on, and report the
base rate with any precision-based metric.

## Takeaways

- **Precision** relates false alarms to true hits, which is what matters when
  positives are rare and only flagged cases are acted on.
- The **PR curve**'s baseline is the base rate. **Average precision** is its
  correct summary; don't use the trapezoidal area.
- AP weights the **top of the ranking**. Here it shows the GBM's advantage
  (`{python} f"{ap['GBM'] / ap['GLM'] - 1:.0%}"`) much more clearly than AUC
  (`{python} f"{auc['GBM'] / auc['GLM'] - 1:.0%}"`).
- With fixed capacity, report **precision and lift at k%**.
- Precision and AP **depend on the base rate**. Never compare them across
  populations with different base rates, and watch them change when the base
  rate drifts.
